appraisal_events.evidence: « Vous comprenez, prince, que je ne voudrais pas laisser une personnalité aussi éminente que la vôtre s'embarquer dans une partie perdue d'avance [...] j'estime que la sagesse est de s'abstenir » ; le prince en conclut : « les négociations n'ont pas fait un pas [...] Je n'ai pas mis la main sur la bonne clef. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Under a lavish compliment to the prince's eminence, Norpois delivers a firm refusal to back his Académie candidacy, and the prince himself decodes the speech as a defeat; the narrator ironizes the delivery by likening Norpois to an old actor gauging his effect.

appraisal_events.evidence: « On peut railler la pédantesque niaiserie avec laquelle les diplomates à la Norpois s'extasient devant une parole officielle [...] Mais leur enfantillage a sa contre-partie : les diplomates savent que [...] les bons sentiments, les beaux discours, les supplications pèsent fort peu » ; cet ordre de vérités « qu'une personne entièrement désintéressée comme ma grand'mère, par exemple, n'eût pas compris »
appraisal_events.explanation: After conceding that Norpois-style diplomacy invites mockery, the narrator turns to vindicate it, crediting Norpois with a hard lucidity about interest and force that the grandmother, and most of humanity, lacks; the concessive-then-corrective structure makes the elevation the dominant move.

status_effects.explanation: Norpois controls the exchange, refusing while appearing to flatter, and the narrator then explicitly credits his school of reading beneath words with a superior grasp of how power actually speaks.
His calculated offering (the cordon de Saint-André) fails to move Norpois and he must admit to himself that he has not found the right key.
He is politely kept outside the Académie, told to abstain rather than be sponsored, and the closing note has him fearing he will die before being elected.

Though used as the figure who could not understand these calculations, she is expressly distinguished from ordinary people whose ignorance comes from lack of intuition: hers is owed to her 'haut désintéressement', which the narrator treats as honorific.

ambiguities: The narrator's stance on Norpois is layered: he opens by granting that one may mock the 'pédantesque niaiserie' and 'enfantillage' of diplomats like Norpois, then reverses with 'Mais' to vindicate their realism. Read here as dominantly elevating, with the mockery surviving as residue rather than as a countervailing movement.

The grandmother's placement is double-edged: her ignorance of interested calculation is both an incapacity and, explicitly, the mark of a high disinterestedness set above the merely unintuitive majority. Read here as mildly honorific, but a reading in which she is simply excluded from worldly competence is also available.
